title: Software Isn’t Losing Its Head. It’s Growing Thousands.
subtitle: Essay · with film
summary: Why strategy firms should turn their methodology into software

essay.text: Every strategy firm is building AI products right now. Most of them are building the wrong thing.
Look across the industry’s AI launches and you’ll find two camps.

The first gives its software a fixed head. A branded dashboard, a bespoke client tool, a polished interface designed to look like the future. It demos beautifully. It’s also frozen the day it ships, while the models and tools around it improve every few months. By the time the client finishes onboarding, the tool is already behind.

The second camp cuts the head off entirely. It wraps the firm’s knowledge in a connector and drops it behind a chat window. This is the “headless” future many claim will kill SaaS: no interface, just a prompt. Flexible, cheap, technically impressive. Then a strategist opens it, stares at the blinking cursor, and has no idea what to ask. A blank box isn’t an interface.
That’s the deeper problem with both camps. They treat the interface as a way to access software, when what matters more is that it’s where the thinking happens.

Strategy isn’t retrieval. Nobody walks into a growth problem knowing the answer and needing a faster way to type it. You find the answer by working through it: framing the question, weighing the trade-offs, and making the call. The human judgment in that process is the whole product. Clients don’t pay for the data. They pay for what an experienced person decides it means.

figure.alt: Three hairline diagrams: points gathered inside a frame, a balance weighing two options, and many lines converging on one point.
figure.caption: Strategy isn’t retrieval: frame the question, weigh the trade-offs, make the call.

essay.text: And yet the tools decide how that thinking happens. A slide forces you into a linear story. A spreadsheet forces you into a grid. A chat window forces you into prose, and asks you to articulate the question before you’ve figured out what it is. Each is a reasonable constraint for some moments and the wrong one for most. We’ve spent decades bending how strategists think around the shape of their tools, and calling the result a deliverable.
If human input is what makes strategy valuable, the interface should serve the way that human thinks, not the other way around.
One head is too rigid. No head is too empty. The answer is more heads.

Many-headed software keeps a single engine underneath: the firm’s data, frameworks, quality bar, and point of view. On top, it grows a new head for every person and every task. The partner preparing for a board meeting gets one view. The analyst stress-testing a market sizing gets another. Each is generated when it’s needed and discarded when it isn’t. Personal front end. Shared back end.

figure.alt: One engine at the centre, labelled data, frameworks, quality bar and point of view, with windows growing from it on drawn lines.
figure.caption: The answer is more heads: one engine, a new head for every person and every task.

essay.text: This isn’t a prettier dashboard. It’s a different idea of what software is. The interface stops being the product and becomes the output.

For strategy firms, that changes the question. It’s no longer “what tool should we build?” It’s “how well have we encoded the way we think?” The firms that answer it won’t ship tools that expire. They’ll ship methodology that compounds.

figure.alt: Two curves over time: tools rise and then fall away, while methodology keeps climbing.
figure.caption: Tools expire. Methodology compounds. An illustration, not data.

title: AI and Crypto: Same Story, Different Technology
subtitle: Essay

essay.heading: The Parallel
essay.text: Crypto and AI share a structural similarity that gets overlooked: in both cases, the underlying technology is real, but the value assigned to companies is driven largely by narrative, presentation, and trust rather than by what the technology actually does. Understanding how that played out in crypto offers a useful lens for evaluating AI companies today.

points.text: Crypto’s core pitch was decentralization, removing the need to trust banks or institutions. But companies like FTX were deeply centralized, dependent on opaque decision-making by a small group. The ideology became a marketing layer that obscured what was actually happening operationally.
Exchanges made confident assertions about reserves, safety, and backing that were never independently audited. When reality diverged from the claims, the damage was catastrophic.
Blockchain was real technology. But most crypto companies weren’t solving real problems, they were applying the tech to extract value through artificial scarcity and narrative-driven demand.

essay.heading: Why AI Faces the Same Pressures
essay.text: AI has something crypto never had: genuine, demonstrable utility. But the same structural vulnerabilities exist:

points.text: Companies can’t reveal what’s actually inside their tools without destroying their competitive advantage. So trust gets built the same way crypto built it, through marketing, UI polish, and storytelling rather than transparency.

Foundation models are essentially a commodity. Everyone is building on similar underlying models. The actual differentiation comes from the wrapper: the interface, the positioning, the narrative about what the tool does. That means the UI is the marketing, and aesthetic experience becomes the primary signal of value for most users.

If an AI tool claims to simulate customer behavior or generate strategic insight, how do you validate that? Companies run internal tests, tune results, and present favorable outcomes. There’s no external standard for what “good output” actually means, which makes it easy to tell a compelling story that’s hard to falsify.

essay.heading: Lessons from Crypto for Evaluating AI Companies

points.text: If a company can’t show you independent validation of their results, not internal benchmarks and not cherry-picked case studies, treat their claims the same way you’d treat an unaudited crypto exchange. The burden of proof should be on them.

points.lead: Separate the technology from the business model.
points.text: AI is real and useful. But that doesn’t mean every company built on top of it is solving a real problem. Ask what the company does that the foundation model alone doesn’t, and whether that wrapper is genuinely valuable or just a story.

points.lead: Watch what the UI is doing.
points.text: A polished interface is a signal, but it can also be a distraction. If the primary value proposition is how good the tool looks to use, that’s worth scrutinizing. Substance and aesthetics can diverge significantly.
